standard.title: Design and prototype user experience
standard.description: design and prototype the user experience of a digital system
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can design the user experience of a digital system, including interface mock-ups and considering user needs (AC9TDI8P07). They have experience with digital design tools. They have not yet prototyped an interactive user experience with clickable flows, or considered all dimensions of UX including emotional, cultural and onboarding experiences.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students design and prototype the user experience of a digital system, including interactive prototypes with clickable flows and consideration of aesthetics, functionality, accessibility, and emotional or cultural user responses.

nodes.label: UX as more than interface — all dimensions of user experience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe what user experience means across its full scope — aesthetics, functionality, onboarding, emotional and cultural responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two distinct dimensions of user experience beyond visual layout (e.g. onboarding experience, emotional response, cultural response, task completion feeling).
nodes.typical_width: Describe the full scope of user experience for a given digital system — including first-use experience, aesthetic and functional response, and emotional or cultural dimensions; explain how each dimension affects users differently.
wider: Evaluate the first-use onboarding experience of an existing digital system — describe what assumptions it makes about users and where those assumptions fail
Examine how users from different cultural backgrounds experience the same digital system differently — identify design choices that create exclusion and what changes would improve inclusivity

response_modes.reason: Students typically think of UX as visual design. Multiple contrasting UX dimensions — onboarding, emotional response, cultural response — expand this to the full scope of the descriptor and are better learned through comparison of distinct contexts than through a definition.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two UX dimensions beyond visual layout
Describes how each dimension affects a user's experience of a specific system
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce UX to visual design cannot complete N2 or N3 — designing for aesthetics + functionality + enjoyment simultaneously, and prototyping a full UX, require the broader conception of UX established at N1.

nodes.label: Designing for aesthetics, functionality and enjoyment
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can design a user experience that integrates aesthetic, functional and enjoyment considerations into a coherent interface.
nodes.minimum_width: Design an interface that addresses both a functional requirement (what the system does) and an aesthetic choice (how it looks and feels); explain the intention behind each choice.
nodes.typical_width: Design a user experience that integrates aesthetics, functionality and the feeling of enjoyment — explain how the design choices work together to create a satisfying user experience; identify trade-offs made between competing design goals.
wider: Design documentation, branding and onboarding materials that extend the UX beyond the screen interactions — explain how consistent branding creates a coherent user experience
Analyse the UX of an existing digital system's getting-started experience — identify what creates a sense of ease or frustration and connect to specific design choices

response_modes.reason: UX design requires students to reason from intent (what experience?) to choices (which aesthetic and functional decisions serve that intent?) — without this reasoning, design choices are arbitrary. Scaffolding the design decision chain prevents the N3 prototype from being a collection of features rather than a designed experience.

success_criteria: Design addresses at least one functional requirement and at least one aesthetic consideration
Student can explain the intention behind specific design choices
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a coherent design intent from N2, the N3 prototype has no basis for its interaction and flow decisions — students prototype arbitrary features rather than a designed experience.

nodes.label: Building an interactive prototype
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can prototype a user experience with interactive elements that simulate clickable flows between screens or views.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a prototype with at least two screens/views linked by a clickable interaction; demonstrate the flow to a peer.
nodes.typical_width: Build a prototype of a simple digital system (e.g. mobile app) using a presentation tool or no-code prototyping tool; include multiple screens with clickable interactions that simulate the user's task completion flow; demonstrate the prototype with a test user and identify one improvement.
wider: Create a high-fidelity prototype that includes edge states — empty states, error states, and success confirmations — not just the happy path
Conduct a structured usability test with a prototype — define tasks, observe users completing them, note where they struggle, and use findings to revise the design

response_modes.reason: A prototype integrates UX understanding (node 1), design intent (node 2) and technical prototype-building skills. Students who understand UX principles often struggle to translate them into an interactive artefact where all the flows must work coherently. The integration challenge is connecting design intent to every specific screen and interaction.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Usability testing with real users is a genuinely rich direction — it produces specific feedback that forces design revision, which is the core UX design skill. Edge states and error handling require students to think about UX beyond the primary flow.
success_criteria: Prototype has at least two screens linked by a clickable interaction
A user can complete at least one task using the prototype without narration from the designer
